stories.headline: Fantasy football stock watch: Boston among players rising; Hurts falling
stories.summary: Matt Bowen lists players who are ascending after one month of play and others trending in the wrong direction.
stories.body:
Four games into the 2026 NFL season, fantasy football managers are starting to get a better feel for their rosters. We see scheme trends developing that impact player upside and usage (both positively and negatively), which can lead to smarter decisions when setting our weekly lineups.

It's also a reminder that the summer hype -- and talk of breakout players -- doesn't always hit once the games are played. Those players we had up high on our draft boards? Some of them are barely hanging on in the lineup, while there are also players emerging at an accelerated rate who need to be in starting slots.

Below are four ascending players and four more who are trending in the opposite direction heading into the Week 5 slate of games.

Stock rising

Denzel Boston, WR, Cleveland Browns

I'd have Boston locked into my lineup as a high-ceiling WR3/flex given his route deployment and explosive-play potential. Boston has scored 12 or more points in three of four games, with a touchdown reception in two. Plus, he's seeing 5.5 targets per game with a route tree that is expanding.

The deep shots from quarterback Deshaun Watson show up on the tape, as Boston has seen eight targets on throws of 15 or more air yards, but the rookie can also uncover on slants, out routes and comebacks. Looking at his play speed and ball-tracking ability, I see big upside for Boston, with the Jets, Ravens and Titans up next.

Deebo Samuel Sr., WR, San Francisco 49ers

Samuel has scored at least 15 points in three of four games, and he is being used exactly how we thought he would be in Kyle Shanahan's offense.

In a tough Week 4 matchup versus the Denver defense, Samuel caught five passes for 26 yards and a touchdown and added 44 yards rushing on three carries, good for 18 fantasy points. Backfield alignments (and carries), screens, crossers and unders. Shanahan will use Samuel, who is a power strider, on concepts that give him a long runway and space to display his vision and physical play style.

Now, the Week 5 matchup versus the Seattle defense isn't ideal, but Samuel gets the Commanders and Falcons, who both rank in the bottom five against opposing wide receivers, in Weeks 6 and 7, respectively. Samuel is a WR3 in 12-team leagues, and the arrow is pointing up for the veteran in this offense.

Kyle Monangai, RB, Chicago Bears

The Bears' ability to dominate game flow and time of possession in the Week 4 win over the Jets boosted the totals for Monangai, who scored a career-high 28 fantasy points, rushing for 146 yards and two touchdowns on 30 carries. He was really decisive with the ball.

Monangai saw seven goal-to-go carries in the game (converting two for touchdowns), while D'Andre Swift struggled in the low red zone. In addition, a second-half Swift fumble prompted coach Ben Johnson to roll with Monangai to close out the game.

With the Packers up next (a team allowing 29 PPG to opposing running backs), and a Bears system that features the run game as a foundational element, both Swift and Monangai should be viewed as viable starters in the RB2/flex range. And that could stick moving forward, depending on weekly matchups.

Malik Washington, WR, Miami Dolphins

We need to talk more about Washington as a potential WR3 in deeper leagues. He has scored 11 or more points in back-to-back games, and he's averaging seven targets per game. Pretty good numbers. And Washington's versatility in the Miami offense creates opportunities within the game plan.

Washington will see targets as an outlet for quarterback Malik Willis on boots and checkdowns, and he can separate from both slot and perimeter alignments. Plus, he is playing that "Deebo" role in Miami, aligning as an I-back to handle rushing attempts. Washington has at least one carry in each of his last three games, and Miami will also get him the ball on fly sweeps and swing screens.

The lack of touchdowns (zero on the season) lowers the upside for Washington, but the usage (27% team target share) and overall deployment give him a stable floor in his upcoming schedule (CIN, BYE, @NYJ).

Stock falling

Jalen Hurts, QB, Philadelphia Eagles

It has been a subpar start to the season for Hurts, who is scoring 16.8 fantasy PPG and averaging 178.3 passing yards. The lack of touchdown production as a runner is really lowering his fantasy ceiling. Hurts is rushing for 26.3 yards per game, but he has just one score on the ground and only two carries inside the 5-yard line. That's rough for managers who drafted Hurts based on his touchdown upside as a dual-threat player.

It doesn't help that the Eagles are banged up right now at critical skill spots, with DeVonta Smith and Saquon Barkley dealing with hamstring injuries. Starting right tackle Lane Johnson retired this week, center Cam Jurgens was traded, and the Eagles' offensive line currently ranks in the bottom five in both pass and run block win rate. Given these factors, in addition to the matchup against the tough Jaguars defense this Sunday in London, Hurts will be outside my top 10 QBs for Week 5.

Omarion Hampton, RB, Los Angeles Chargers

This one is tough for me because I was all-in on Hampton this summer as the lead back in Mike McDaniel's offense. However, Hampton is scoring 11.2 fantasy PPG, and we saw L.A. move to a true committee approach this past week in the loss to the Seahawks.

Hampton managed to save his day with a late touchdown in that one, finishing with 13.3 points on 11 touches, but it was Keaton Mitchell who saw the most action (15 touches), with Kimani Vidal also getting in the mix (seven touches). And that's my concern moving forward with Hampton, as his nine carries versus Seattle were a season low.

I understand the Chargers' coaches here, too. This team is off to a 0-4 start, which leads to personnel changes. I've seen it firsthand in the league. Hampton is averaging only 4.0 YPC this season, and he hasn't impacted the offense as a receiver (7.3 yards per game).

With another tough matchup in Week 5 versus the Broncos, managers should play Hampton only as a touchdown-dependent flex, and this Chargers backfield rotation could keep him there for a while.

Daniel Jones, QB, Indianapolis Colts

Jones was a candidate this summer as a possible matchup-based QB1 in 12-team leagues or as a starter in superflex formats. But Jones is scoring just 9.1 fantasy PPG, down from the 17.4 he posted in 2025. The movement traits (and rushing totals) are limited because of his recovery from the Achilles injury he suffered last season. Plus, without Alec Pierce (IR/heel), the Colts are missing that vertical element in the pass game, which squeezes the field for the quarterback.

Through four games, Jones is averaging 188.5 passing yards per game, and he's 1-for-5 on throws of 20 or more air yards. Plus, Jones has rushed for one score while averaging just 5.3 yards per game on the ground, and he has managed only three touchdown passes (compared with four interceptions).

Pierce is eligible to return from IR in Week 7, which would give this pass game a lift. But I still don't see enough here for Jones to be played as anything more than a bye-week fill-in in deeper superflex formats.

David Montgomery, RB, Houston Texans

I really wanted this Texans run game to go this season. The team traded for Montgomery and they also addressed the offensive line. Get the running back with the contact balance and the lateral agility to play downhill behind an upgraded front.

It's not happening here.

Montgomery did score 28.9 fantasy points in Week 1, but he had three touchdowns in that game versus Buffalo, while producing only 79 total yards on 23 touches. And the numbers have really declined over his last three games, with Montgomery averaging 2.5 YPC and only 38.3 yards from scrimmage. More importantly, Montgomery hasn't found the end zone since Week 1. The result? He scored just 5.2 fantasy PPG in Weeks 2-4.

I don't see enough movement up front from a Houston offensive line with a run block win rate of 70.9% (28th in the league), and Montgomery has seen only 10.3 touches per game over his last three. With his upcoming schedule (@TEN, @JAX, NYG), Montgomery is (at best) a touchdown-dependent flex option.

stories.headline: F1 cars to get software update after Malaysia 'bug' to prevent repeat at future races
stories.summary: Following last weekend's farcical formation lap at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the FIA will introduce new wet-weather engine software in time for the United States Grand Prix later this month.
stories.body:
Following last weekend's farcical formation lap at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, the FIA will introduce new wet-weather engine software in time for the United States Grand Prix later this month.

The Bahrain Grand Prix, which was hosted at Malaysia's Sepang circuit, was the first wet race under F1's new power unit regulations in 2026 and revealed a considerable oversight in the FIA software that polices the deployment of electric power on each car.

Described as "totally unacceptable" and "horrible" by drivers, a bug in the software supplied to all teams by the FIA resulted in multiple cars losing power as they followed the Safety Car at slow speeds on the formation lap.

The bug resulted in multiple cars losing drive coming out of the slow Turn 9 corner as the software prevented the use of electric power at a point where the internal combustion engine was struggling at low revs to spool the turbo and regain full power.

Some drivers were able to return to a normal speed once the system reset itself, while others, such as Lewis Hamilton, had to pull to the side of the track to restart their power unit.

"The review concluded that some cars running on low engine RPM [Revolutions Per Minute] in certain circuit sectors where a 250kW [kilowatt] power reduction was applied experienced a loss of power beyond the original intent and that could not be recovered in those sectors," an FIA statement said ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

Once the issue was detected, the start of the race was suspended for a second time as the FIA investigated the bug.

Within five minutes of the suspension of the race, the FIA had released updated software to all teams to address the problem.

Over the following 30 minutes, the FIA worked with the teams to ensure the software was properly installed on all cars, allowing racing to get back underway 48 minutes after the issue first became apparent.

- Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

- Valtteri Bottas cycles impressive 400km from Malaysia to Singapore Grand Prix: 'Snakes were pretty chill'

- Max Verstappen says F1 paddock 'less stressful' without Christian Horner

The same software issued to the teams during the suspension of the race in Malaysia will be in use at this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix before a further update will be released ahead of the United States Grand Prix on Oct. 25.

Although the FIA countered suggestions the software had not been tested at all prior to Sunday's race, its investigation recommended additional testing be granted in the future.

"The review also recommended that measures would be implemented for testing of the software, recognising that opportunities for testing are limited, to make it robust as possible," the statement added. "The FIA , together with the teams and Power Unit Manufacturers (PUMs), will continue to strengthen Power Unit software testing and verification capabilities, enhancing the overall validation process through independent assessment and collaborative feedback, including input from the supplier of the standardised Electronics Control Unit (ECU).

"The FIA would like to address comments suggesting that the software had not been tested prior to its deployment. Before implementation, teams and Power Unit manufacturers conducted simulation exercises to validate the software package, which was subsequently tested in full-scale running during Free Practice 1 sessions at both the Belgian Grand Prix and the Dutch Grand Prix."

stories.headline: Wysh List: What NHL execs think of ESPN's top 100 player rankings
stories.summary: Who was too high or too low according to actual team personnel and players? Plus, winners and losers of the week, key upcoming games and more.
stories.body:
"Why do you do this to yourselves?"

That was the first reaction from an NHL general manager as he perused the latest NHL Rank, the top 100 player list that publishes at the start of every season. It was a reaction that signaled some discontent with the ranking -- and he wasn't alone -- as well as a twinge of sympathy for the inevitable backlash that accompanies such an undertaking.

Here's the method to this madness: 15 individuals from the ESPN hockey family, from front-facing talents to ink-drenched scribes to analytics virtuosi, submitted their own ranking of the top 100 NHL players based on how well they're expected to perform in the 2026-27 regular season. Those ballots are combined to come up with a final Top 100.

So, in theory, this is a projection of greatness rather than a coronation for past efforts. Does that explain why Connor Hellebuyck, currently suspended by the Winnipeg Jets after a trade request, could be ranked 22nd if he's not even playing? Well, no, it doesn't, but then there are plenty of other questions for those who debated it this week.

I spoke with several NHL executives about this year's ranking. They had questions of their own.

"Why is Alex Ovechkin ranked here? Like, at all?" one executive asked.

The Washington Capitals' captain was ranked No. 78.

"He barely skates anymore. Ovechkin being on this list is silly. What year is this?"

Oh, c'mon ... let the man retire with dignity!

Another NHL executive believed there was another glaring gaffe in the ranking: New York Islanders phenom Matthew Schaefer at No. 16. Last season's rookie of the year had 59 points in 82 games while skating 24:41 per night. That ice time ranked 14th among all defensemen, and many of those defensemen who skated more finished well behind the 19-year-old in this ranking.

"Not many young defensemen have that kind of impact, that early," they said.

Speaking of Schaefer: "So two of the top six defensemen in the NHL got cut by Hockey Canada? Because Colton Parayko, Travis Sanheim and Drew Doughty are nowhere to be found on this list, and they all played in the Olympics," pondered one NHL executive, in reference to Schaefer and Evan Bouchard of the Edmonton Oilers.

(For what it's worth, Doughty made last year's list at No. 54 while the others did not.)

A few other reactions to our player ranking from NHL front office suits:

Two execs believed that the voters had succumbed to the siren's song of scoring, rather than accounting for the actual sway players have over their team's fortunes. "I think you have some high rankings on players who have more points scored than actual impact," one GM said. Another team exec lamented: "Too many empty-calorie point guys that don't drive winning," while specifically calling out Montreal winger Cole Caufield (25th).
A few players were cited by multiple NHL executives as being undervalued in this ranking: New York Rangers defenseman Adam Fox (51), Vegas Golden Knights winger Mark Stone (73) and Tampa Bay Lightning winger Brandon Hagel (55). "Brandon Hagel is a superstar, and people don't realize it. Way too low," one executive said.
More than one exec noted that our ranking of the 100 best players didn't exactly honor the reigning Stanley Cup champions, the Carolina Hurricanes. Center Sebastian Aho (48) was the only Cane to crack the top 50, and he was down from 28th on last year's list. Jaccob Slavin (62), Seth Jarvis (74), Andrei Svechnikov (84) and Nikolaj Ehlers (96) also made the cut. "Where's anyone from the best line from the reigning Cup winners?" one executive asked, referring to the trio of Taylor Hall, Logan Stankoven and Jackson Blake.

I'm not going to deny there are a few shots that missed the net on this list. Schaefer is way too high. So is Martin Necas of the Colorado Avalanche at 24th; he had a career year skating 82% of the time with Nathan MacKinnon -- a luxury not afforded to several wingers ranked behind him. Would I have Brandt Clarke ranked ahead of Shea Theodore? I would not. Would I have had Darren Raddysh on this list at all, let alone at No. 90? I also would not.

On the flippity flop, Leo Carlson (36th) and Stone should be much higher. I would have liked Florida defenseman Seth Jones somewhere on this list -- although perhaps the toxic stink cloud from his time with the Blackhawks still follows him in South Florida despite helping the Panthers to their second Stanley Cup win.

But here's my scorching hot take on this year's NHL Rank on ESPN. Prepare yourself. Maybe get a tall glass of milk to handle the ghost pepper sear of this take.

The NHL Rank list is overall pretty ... good?

Qualms and quibbles aside, the top of the list seems about right. Proper respect was given to emerging talents (Macklin Celebrini at No. 4 and Nick Suzuki at No. 19) and established stars (Sidney Crosby, hanging tough at No. 23). Heck, we even found a way to get Evgeni Malkin in at No. 100, so Pittsburgh fans can finally extinguish the torches they light whenever this ranking dropped without him in it.

During my conversations around the league about the list, I found out I wasn't alone.

"This looks absolutely fine to me. I've got nothing to criticize here," one NHL assistant general manager said.

An NHL veteran player who scanned the list agreed.

"I think everyone is actually where they should be," the player said when shown the top 100. "It's a nice list. No notes."

Based on my texts, my inbox and my mentions, everyone else had more than enough notes to share. Some even without profanity!

Jump ahead:

Winners, losers of the week

Favorite on-ice moment

Must-see games

Puck headlines

WINNERS AND LOSERS
Winner: Alex Ovechkin
Last season, Ovechkin explicitly didn't want a farewell tour because he felt his pursuit of Wayne Gretzky's record in 2024-25 overshadowed everything about the Capitals, including his teammates. But after deciding in the summer that this season would be his last in the NHL, Ovi decided to just put the issue to bed early, sparing his teammates from questions about his status for the next 80-plus games.

It also sets up the NHL for a one-of-a-kind farewell tour. Consider other recent transcendent stars. Wayne Gretzky didn't let his fate be known until there were just a few games left in the 1998-99 season. Mario Lemieux played until he couldn't. Jaromir Jagr was an afterthought on the Calgary Flames before spending the next decade in Kladno, Czechia. Ovechkin will visit 31 other teams for the final time, giving fans the chance to react to his last NHL days.

That includes what could be the emotional apex of his season on April 4 in Washington's home finale against Sidney Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and the Pittsburgh Penguins. If you don't have tickets and want to attend, prepare to sell a kidney.

Loser: Brady Tkachuk
The Florida Panthers didn't have a regulation loss in their first four games (2-0-2). Their losses were on the roster. Aleksander Barkov's lower-body injury thankfully wasn't as bad as feared, but their best player is still on the shelf for about six weeks. Brad Marchand was helped off the ice Tuesday after collisions with the net and the boards in Los Angeles. As of this writing, his status was unknown, but it didn't look good.

Another point of concern through four games: Brady Tkachuk has put out more podcasts (two) than put up points (zero), despite leading the Panthers with 11 shots. Granted, the loss of Barkov in Game 2 affected him -- witness Sam Reinhart also sporting goose eggs on his stat line through four games -- but Tkachuk was acquired to help the Panthers through significant lineup losses like they had last season. Plus, he has had to watch his old friends in Ottawa thriving in his absence.

Tkachuk will be fine. But it's not the start he or the Panthers wanted statistically.

Winner: GQ covers hockey
It's always interesting to see how a writer who doesn't cover hockey processes our silly little sport. Nick Remsen of GQ profiled San Jose Sharks star Macklin Celebrini, and gave NHL fans some artful new descriptions of backhand shots ("[He] pushed the puck into the net with the convex side of his blade, body twisting with near balletic torque...") and routine goal celebrations ("He was so happy after ricocheting a puck into the net's far outer edge that he all but flung himself into the sideboards...").

Loser: GQ makes it weird
Given the "Heated Rivalry" and "Off Campus" phenomenon and the NHL's now shuttered "Hot For Hockey" experiment, it's not out of bounds to ask someone like Macklin about the para-social relationship between fans and players. Where things got weird in the Celebrini profile: Asking about the "fan fiction element" in his fandom. Given the content in some of those stories, that question felt invasive and put him in an awkward spot.

Celebrini understandably punted on the answer, which isn't something for which he should have to answer for anyway. Besides, it's not as if fan fiction involving NHL players started with Macklin Celebrini.

Winner: Dylan Larkin drama
A few sources around the league I spoke with previously didn't believe we'd see Larkin wear a Detroit sweater again, but the now-former Red Wings captain returned to the lineup from injury Tuesday night, his first game since requesting a trade from Detroit. The fans booed him as they booed him on opening night when he was introduced in street clothes; Larkin responded with a goal and an assist to reignite the dormant Detroit offense.

There were some cheers interspersed with the boos when he was announced as the No. 1 star. After the game, Larkin said, "I'm just happy to be a hockey player today and go out and try to help the team win."

Give Larkin this credit: He has spoken to reporters. He has faced the fans. He wore a uniform that he has asked to no longer wear. How this all ends up is anyone's guess, but we're here for the soap opera: "As The Winged Wheel Turns."

Loser: No-trade clauses
The aftermath of Larkin's trade request was put into sharp relief last week when NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said the league is monitoring how players are using their no-movement and no-trade clauses. Larkin, then Detroit's captain, asked out with five years left on an eight-year contract, and limited the field of suitors to three teams with his no-trade clause.

Just like how the NHL enacted offside reviews because one player (Matt Duchene) was a country mile offside and the officials missed it, Larkin's trade request appears to have lit the fuse for this potentially contentious labor dispute.

What I can report: Bettman is speaking to players to get feedback on the way trade protection is currently being used and potential changes to the system down the line. It'll be fascinating to hear how they feel about Larkin's gambit.

Favorite on-ice moment

It's always fascinating to see what the league's preeminent agitators use for material. Ottawa forward Nick Cousins pantomiming the letter "C" and pointing to his chest as he taunts Dylan Larkin getting the captaincy stripped from him? Chef's kiss, especially if you want to add the subtext of having reminded Larkin that he's stuck in some kind of trade demand purgatory.

Must-see games coming up

Toronto Maple Leafs at Vegas Golden Knights

Thursday, 10 p.m. ET | ESPN+

The vibes are good for the Leafs. They're 2-2-0. Auston Matthews scored an overtime winner against Nashville in a game that saw No. 1 pick Gavin McKenna finally hit the scoresheet. But starting with this game against old pal Mitch Marner and the Golden Knights, we're going to learn about more about Toronto: The Leafs are at Colorado, at Utah and then get Buffalo at home.

Edmonton Oilers at San Jose Sharks

Saturday, 4 p.m. ET | ESPN+

Celebrini is day-to-day, and one hopes he's available for a showdown against Connor McDavid. But no matter his status: This is a four-point divisional game for the Sharks, and if they're going to be a playoff team then these are the games they need to win.

Colorado Avalanche at Dallas Stars

Tuesday, 8:30 p.m. ET | ESPN

The first meeting between the two best regular-season teams in the Central Division last season. Three of their four games in 2025-26 went to a shootout. An early test for both teams.

From your hockey friends at ESPN

Ryan Clark went to Houston to find out why that city believes it deserves an NHL expansion team more than Austin, Texas, does. Said Mayor John Whitmire on what the city will do to get a team: "We're not going to start selling dope out of an arena or anything. But if it's lawful, we'll pull that trigger."
Sean Allen looks at hits and blocks in fantasy hockey, and who could be the most valuable players this season to that end.
Kalan Hooks with a wild story out of New Jersey, as a youth hockey team owner is under fire after threatening to suspend the children on his under-10 hockey team after their parents created their own merchandise.
Finally, Rachel Kryshak has a deep dive into which NCAA teams have the most high-end talent. How did we end up with so many kids named "Ryker" playing hockey?

Jersey Foul

I appreciate the integration of Larkin's name into this Protest Jersey about his trade request. Much more impressive than just using the "L" and taping the word "LOSER" on the back or just covering the whole thing with the word "TRAITOR," which is what other fans decided to do.

Puck headlines
DATELINE: TEAM USA GROUP CHAT
One of the greatest bits of hockey lore going these days is the power of the U.S. men's Olympic team group chat, which has been credited with having players like Winnipeg Jets goalie Connor Hellebuyck demand a trade to the U.S.

Gold medalist Vincent Trocheck of the Utah Mammoth says he believes its power is overstated.

"I think people make it a bigger thing than it is," he told me this week. "Obviously, people want the headlines, but the whole Canada thing or guys wanting out of Canada that are from the U.S., I think it was more situational than it was anything else."

But is there a thriving group chat among the players?

"There's one from Team USA. But not, like, a trade talk one," he said. "It's been dormant for a little bit. It's sad. I might have to fire it back up."

DATELINE: CONNOR HELLEBUYCK
It was a bit surprising when Jets GM Kevin Cheveldayoff didn't rule out the possibility that Hellebuyck could remain with the team after going public with a trade demand.

But one former teammate of the star goaltender I spoke with actually didn't rule it out.

The thinking here: Hellebuyck will eventually grow frustrated with losing pay after having been suspended by the Jets, as it has been reported he'll lose around $39,000 a day. But more than that, he's still on friendly terms with his teammates -- some of them neighbors -- who theoretically would welcome back the multitime Vezina Trophy winner if he decides to pull a Larkin and suit up again.

DATELINE: UTAH MAMMOTH
One sign the Mammoth are really starting to thrive in Salt Lake City? The lack of enemy fans in the stands. Team president Chris Armstrong told me that when Utah opened its season against the Blackhawks at home, there were very few Chicago fans in the building "in comparison to the inaugural season" in Salt Lake City.

"I feel like maybe that people are switching their allegiance to the Mammoth now," Armstrong said.

If they keep playing the way they're playing to start the season, who wouldn't?

The Wysh List is created by senior writer Greg Wyshynski and appears every Thursday on ESPN.com and the ESPN app.

stories.headline: Saints trade ruckman to Cats, chase on for star Swan
stories.summary: Geelong have brokered a trade for St Kilda ruckman Rowan Marshall, further depleting the Cats' draft stocks as Swans defender Nick Blakey eyes a move.
stories.body:
St Kilda have pulled the trigger on a deal to send contracted ruckman Rowan Marshall to Geelong, as the Cats and other rival clubs circle Sydney star Nick Blakey.

Geelong traded pick No. 14 in this year's draft for the disenchanted 30-year-old and a third-round selection in 2028 on Thursday afternoon.

New Zealand-born Marshall had requested a move to the Cats for a second straight year after St Kilda recruited Tom De Koning to become their first-choice ruckman.

Cats football boss Andrew Mackie on Monday indicated an unwillingness to part with their first-round pick for Marshall after the Saints asked for a player to be attached to the trade.

St Kilda football boss Lenny Hayes hailed the fair return for Marshall, who has played 177 AFL games since being a rookie pick at age 21.

"We are pleased to have achieved (adequate compensation) by bringing in another first round selection, alongside our existing pick at eight," Hayes said.

Geelong needed to bolster their ruck stocks, with Rhys Stanley retiring and 21-year-old Mitchell Edwards still finding his feet at the level.

The Cats are among five clubs eyeing Nick Blakey as the Swans defender tests the water for a possible trade.

The 2024 All-Australian was one of five players who served a club-imposed ban through the AFL finals for breaching the club's behavioural standards at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne.

The 26-year-old has since been linked to a move despite being signed to Sydney until 2031.

Swans list boss Chris Keane said the club had not been told Blakey was meeting with rival clubs this week, but remained in talks with his manager Robbie D'Orazio.

"As we sit here right now, these are all hypotheticals," he told Trade Radio.

"It's certainly not something we've actively pursued, and we feel confident that he could walk back into our footy club.

"But given the calibre of player that he is, and the fact that he is contracted for five more years, we feel like making any deal happen would be significantly challenging."

Blakey's preferred option is reportedly Geelong, but the Cats have limited draft capital after executing trades for Marshall and Essendon's Jordan Ridley.

North Melbourne have expressed interest for Blakey, whose father John played in the Kangaroos' 1996 and 1999 premierships across 224 club games.

Essendon are another suitor, with Blakey's former mentors Mark McVeigh and John Longmire joining the club and the Bombers boasting salary cap room following the exits of Zach Merrett and Ridley.

"We haven't had any indication off Nick's management that he's looking to leave Sydney," Essendon list boss Matt Rosa told Trade Radio.

"But certainly we've had some discussions internally and we'll continue to do that."

Blakey has reportedly already met with Gold Coast coach Damien Hardwick, while St Kilda are also expected to make contact.

Any trade for Blakey would likely need to be approved by a club board, given the ongoing police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the hotel.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney, star midfielder Chad Warner, tagger James Jordon and Blakey were interviewed by police but no charges have been laid.

Riley Bice, another Swan banned for round 24 and the finals campaign, is not being investigated.

In other developments, young Hawk Aidan Schubert has agreed to be traded to Gold Coast in a separate deal that is expected to allow Ben King join Hawthorn as a free agent.

The Suns' 72-hour window to match the Hawks' offer for King or accept compensation, likely pick No. 7 in the draft, ends at 4.15pm (AEDT) on Friday.

The Western Bulldogs are yet to file free agency paperwork for Port Adelaide's Zak Butters ahead of Friday afternoon's deadline.

Port can accept draft compensation, which would currently deliver pick No.5, or match the Bulldogs' offer and force a trade.

The trade period closes on Wednesday evening.

stories.headline: Silva rises in P4P women's top 10, making most of golden opportunity
stories.summary: After winning UFC women's flyweight title, Silva rises in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
The women's flyweight division might be the most stacked weight class in the UFC, and Natalia Silva wears the gold.

Silva was too fast, too precise and too elusive for Wang Cong in the UFC 332 main event on Saturday, and as a result, the 29-year-old from Brazil captured the vacant 125-pound title. She moves up one position to No. 4 in the ESPN women's pound-for-pound rankings.

Silva is one of seven flyweights in the women's top 10. The division with the next most pound-for-pound elites is lightweight, with three fighters in the men's rankings.

The top two fighters on the women's list are Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the UFC title last month while healing shoulder and back injuries, and Zhang Weili, a two-time former strawweight titlist who last fought at flyweight, in an unsuccessful challenge of Shevchenko in November.

Aside from Silva, there are three other UFC flyweights in the top 10 (Alexa Grasso, Manon Fiorot and Erin Blanchfield), and the rankings also include PFL 125-pounder Dakota Ditcheva.

UFC women's bantamweight champion Kayla Harrison has been missing from these rankings for the past few months because, with no fights since June 2025, she is ineligible. But Harrison will return from neck surgery to defend her title against former two-division champion and consensus GOAT Amanda Nunes at UFC 334 on Nov. 14.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 7. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 5

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Previous ranking: 4

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her upcoming bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. 2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

UFC heavyweight

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

UFC lightweight champion

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

Record: 17-1

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

9. Ciryl Gane

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

stories.headline: NRL: Spencer Leniu signs with Eels after early Roosters release
stories.summary: Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.
stories.body:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in their 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith from 2021-2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 per year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The westward move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Eels general manager of football Mark O'Neill shared his delight at signing one of the game's "premier enforcers".

"We're thrilled to have Spencer join the Parramatta Eels and become part of what we're building at this club," O'Neill said in a statement.

"He's one of the elite middle forwards in the game and has consistently performed on the biggest stages throughout his career.

The exit of Leniu adds to the exodus of stars from the Roosters premiership lineup.

Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

Roosters coach Trent Robinson said Leniu had been a strong contributor during his time at the club.

"Spencer has brought a lot to our group over the last three years, both through the way he plays and the energy and personality he brings every day," Robinson said in a statement on Thursday.

"He brings an intensity and competitiveness to everything he does, and he challenges the people around him to be better.

"To see him finish his time here as a premiership winner is something he should be really proud of, and something we'll always share together."

With his departure announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

""I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," said Leniu.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

stories.headline: The Warriors need Yaxel Lendeborg's fast-tracked development
stories.summary: The Golden State Warriors have high hopes for the No. 11 pick after several failed lottery picks.
stories.body:
THE WEEK BEFORE training camp, every Golden State Warriors player gathered at Jimmy Butler's mansion in San Diego and competed in a handful of pickup games.

In his lone game paired with Stephen Curry and Draymond Green, rookie wing Yaxel Lendeborg found himself near the elbow during a frontcourt inbound. As the ball was delivered to Green up top, Curry cut toward Lendeborg to set a back screen. Both defenders remained with Curry; Lendeborg, sensing it, slipped backdoor and received a pass from Green for an uncontested dunk.

"'That's all year! All year!'" Green and Curry roared at Lendeborg with ferocity, according to the rookie. "Super loud and aggressive."

In Lendeborg's mind, he made the simple read within the flow, using Curry's gravity for two easy points. It represented something far bigger for Green and Curry. Their newest weapon was already recognizing and leveraging the patterns that make the Warriors' offense hum, signaling a readiness to help the team win before the two franchise legends age out of the league.

"It looked like we had been playing together for a long time," Green said.

On their final draft board in June, the Warriors -- who owned the No. 11 pick -- had Lendeborg and Arizona guard Brayden Burries ranked neck-and-neck, behind the consensus group of prospects up top. If Burries was there, team sources have indicated they would've drafted the 20-year-old combo guard for his upside. He had fans all over the organization.

But the Milwaukee Bucks, selecting 10th, took away that option. The Warriors quickly pivoted to Lendeborg, adding the older prospect they believed fit their immediate timeline and urgency of Curry's final seasons.

"He's massive," Butler said. "Just a big human being."

At 24 years old and 241 pounds, standing 6-foot-9 with a 7-foot-4 wingspan, Lendeborg has the size and power of a mid-prime wing on a Warriors roster that is currently thin and injured at that spot, waiting for Butler and Moses Moody to return from lengthy rehabs for serious knee injuries.

Lendeborg won over Steve Kerr in the predraft process, impressing the Warriors coach during a film session because of his knowledge of the game paired with charisma and his willingness to learn.

"Unbelievably coachable," Kerr said of Lendeborg after Tuesday night's preseason win over the Los Angeles Lakers.

The organization has been impressed that, after a long national title run at Michigan that included an MCL and ankle sprain in the NCAA tournament, Lendeborg took his offseason work seriously, played in eight summer league games and led them to a Las Vegas title.

Then he showed up at training camp and Kerr inserted him into the starting lineup, showing a belief that he can be a small forward in a lineup that includes Green and a center or a power forward next to Green in smaller groupings.

Newcomers either typically get the Warriors' unique style, offensive flow and Curry-centric approach or don't -- and it's obvious immediately. Andre Iguodala and Juan Toscano-Anderson did. Kelly Oubre and James Wiseman didn't.

The Warriors' belief in Lendeborg comes at a time when the franchise is desperate for young talent that helps win in Curry's final years while better positioning them for a tricky rebuild.

"He's going to play a ton," Kerr told ESPN. "Frankly, he deserves it. He's one of our best players already."

LENDEBORG INITIALLY DECLARED for the 2025 draft after two seasons at UAB, averaging 17.7 points and 11.4 rebounds as a small-ball center his last season there. General manager Mike Dunleavy and a group of front office members met Lendeborg at the combine in Chicago. Their feedback: He was behaving "like a jackass," Lendeborg recalled in a summer league interview with ESPN.

"I was like, damn, I did that bad?" Lendeborg laughed.

It wasn't clear then whether Lendeborg was even a first-round pick. There was a belief he needed to improve his work habits and sharpen his approach. He withdrew from the draft, transferred to Michigan, morphed into a dominant force on a national title team -- averaging 15.1 points and 6.8 rebounds per game while shooting 51.5% from the field -- and returned to the combine with a rising stock.

"The biggest thing for sure is just practice overall," Lendeborg said. "I never took practice serious [until Michigan]."

Kerr commented recently about Lendeborg's constant presence in the gym. Teammates have embraced what they say is a genuine personality and curiosity, as Lendeborg regularly asks questions to help fast track his growth.

"I don't think he's afraid," Curry said. "It's a lot for a rookie to absorb all this information and process it. He's open-minded. He's listening. You can tell he's locked in mentally."

But there's still a natural "goofiness," as several in the building have described it, that seeps onto the court and will cause inevitable growing pains for the rookie. One possession into the preseason, the referee had to ask Lendeborg to tuck in his jersey. The coaches particularly mention the "nonchalant" nature impacting his defensive focus.

"The biggest thing I see that he needs work with is being in a stance," Kerr said. "Off-ball, he tends to stand up a little bit. The other night against the Clippers, he was casual and Rui [Hachimura] came off a couple pindowns and he wasn't quite prepared."

The Hachimura scouting report is clear -- run him off the line. The Warriors went over it before the preseason game against the Clippers. But Lendeborg sagged off and gave him a few jumpers. Green expressed a bit of on-court frustration and reiterated a need for Lendeborg to focus more on the defensive end when the rookie texted the veteran for advice after the first game.

It was also a problem two days before during an open intrasquad scrimmage. Lendeborg gifted De'Anthony Melton and Gui Santos space on the perimeter and they stepped into easy 3s. Green was frustrated. Someone in the gym had to loudly remind him: "He's a rookie!"

"Everybody [in the NBA] can shoot," Lendeborg said. "I've been a guy that's always given up the jump shot and kind of baited players to go into the paint and attack me. Here I can't do that."

Lendeborg said he became comfortable at Michigan in a switch everything scheme. He's rangy and fluid with shot-blocking instincts and felt comfortable against guards, wings and bigs. But this isn't college.

"The switch attack offense in the NBA is very, very advanced," assistant coach Frank Vogel told ESPN. "So if you're just going to rely only on switching, it's not all about guarding the guy you switched onto. It's about guarding the exchange, giving up roll behinds, giving up hip taps, slip outs."

Vogel was hired this summer to take control of a Warriors defense that has slipped. Players, coaches and front office members have raved about Vogel's early impact and attention to detail. That includes regular lessons for Lendeborg.

"It's more like a chase over, fight over kind of game [in the NBA]," Lendeborg said. "I've never really done that, so I'm still trying to navigate that. Then some of the rotations off-ball as well. Just, like, when to help, when not to help. Those kind of things have been confusing me a little bit."

There are defensive areas where Lendeborg's size will naturally help. He has 18 rebounds in 40 preseason minutes and said after his second game he felt it was easier to rebound in the NBA because the paint isn't as packed and the opposing rebounders seem "lazy."

"In a league where the big shoulder offense of just plowing into a guy to create space, he's going to be one of them guys that you're not going to be able to punk," Vogel said. "And that's going to be a big benefit to us."

Most rookies, as Vogel put it, arrive "really thin" and need at least a couple years in the weight room before it's feasible for them to survive when the NBA game ramps up physically. But Lendeborg is already in the OG Anunoby and Paolo Banchero weight class (240-plus pounds). His body is ready. The veterans and coaches are now just trying to train the mind.

"What does Shai [Gilgeous-Alexander] do?" Kerr said. "What does Damian Lillard do if you get switched on him? You're guarding a big, know the scouting report -- is Chet Holmgren going to pop and hit 3s? What's his tendency? Pick a guy. You get switched on to Luka [Doncic]. Are you ready for that pump fake or is he going to goad you into three free throws? That only comes with experience and watching League Pass and getting to know the league."

THE WARRIORS DON'T have the greatest recent track record of developing lottery rookies, but they believe the timing and situation is far different than it was with Jonathan Kuminga, whom the Warriors drafted with the No. 7 pick in 2021 and traded in February after never finding the correct developmental direction and alignment during five turbulent seasons..

Lendeborg is actually a month older than Kuminga. The Warriors drafted Kuminga the same year Lendeborg was beginning the second of three seasons at Arizona Western College in Yuma. His late teens, early 20s growing pains were ironed out in junior college and eventually high-stakes Division I.

Front offices often shy away from drafting older prospects early because of the concern about a limited upside. Lendeborg is already 24. But if he is an immediate high-level contributor at a position of great need, as the Warriors believe he will be, they will get his age 24 to 27 seasons on a bargain four-year, $28.1 million deal.

"We're in a position now [as opposed to past seasons] where we can be thinking of development," Kerr said. "Not just for Yaxel, but our whole group. We are not in the [championship] conversation. So let's see what we can do as a group to kind of reestablish what we stand for and how we operate and new beginnings in a lot of ways. All of that is really exciting to me. And Yaxel's a big part of that."

Lendeborg has no issue embracing the spotlight and pressure. He has declared he can average 15 points, six rebounds and four assists in his first season. He believes he could win Rookie of the Year.

Asked during one of his many livestreams this summer about Phoenix Suns wing Dillon Brooks, he responded: "I'm finna give Dillon Brooks belt, man. Stop playing." The Warriors face the Suns on Oct. 24, their third regular-season game.

"You can also see his youth with his comments in the media," Kerr said. "Our fans are going to love listening to him and he's going to say some stuff that he may have to retract and hold back. But I love it. I love him. I love guys like that. We always encourage everyone to be themselves and he's got a really great personality."

But that comes with an added spotlight, especially when playing for a brand like the Warriors next to a teammate like Curry.

"The nature of our league, social media and all the microscope is that they'll expect him to be a 20-8-6 guy right out the gate or whatever number you put on him," Curry said.

"But his job is to block all that out. He will know if he's impactful. He will know if he's helping win games. The stats and the numbers will follow. It's our job to protect him in that."

Still, the Warriors are struggling to contain their excitement and temper expectations for Lendeborg, who has popped off for 21 points, 18 rebounds, five assists and two blocks in his first 40 preseason minutes.

"He's obviously a winner," Curry said. "He had a successful year in college in the big role he had. He has great feel. He has great size. He's been shooting it really well. You can tell he wants to make the right play. For our offense and game plan, that's usually going to shine."

stories.headline: Max Dowman presented with three Guinness World Records after breakout Arsenal season
stories.summary: Max Dowman has added three Guinness World Records to his growing list of achievements despite not turning 17 until this coming December.
stories.body:
Max Dowman has added three Guinness World Records to his growing list of achievements despite not turning 17 until this coming December.

The Arsenal winger enjoyed a breakout season in 2025-26, making 13 senior appearances and scoring a memorable clincher in the Premier League against Everton.

That goal -- in which Dowman ran from his own half, beat two players and tapped into an empty net with Jordan Pickford having come up for a corner -- came with the youngster aged just 16 years and 73 days old, officially making him the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history.

Dowman had already broken another world record prior to that. At the age of 15 years and 308 days, he was introduced as a substitute in Arsenal's 3-0 win at Slavia Prague and became the youngest player ever to make a Champions League appearance.

In fact, no 15-year-old other than him has ever played in the competition.

There was more glory, and one more world record, to come. With Arsenal having won their first Premier League title since 2004, Dowman collected his winner's medal when he was 16 years and 144 days old -- the youngest ever to do so.

Phil Foden was the previous holder of the award, as he was part of Manchester City's 100-point team when he was just 17 years old.

Dowman narrowly missed out on a fourth world record last season having made his debut -- and won a penalty -- against Leeds United at 15 years and 235 days old, just under two months older than teammate Ethan Nwaneri was when he made his debut against Brentford in 2022.

- Mikel Arteta signs new four-year Arsenal contract

- Ian Darke's early Premier League impressions for all 20 teams

- Myles Lewis-Skelly, Estêvão, Yan Diomande make 2026 Golden Boy shortlist

The winger has carried his good form into this season, having scored twice in Arsenal's 4-2 Carabao Cup win over Ipswich in September.

Mikel Arteta's side return from the international break with a repeat of the fixture in which Dowman made his debut: Leeds at home, on Saturday.

stories.headline: WNBA playoffs 2026: After another early exit, what's next for Fever?
stories.summary: Despite a dominant offense and Caitlin Clark's return, the Fever suffered another early playoff exit. What's next for Indiana?
stories.body:
INDIANAPOLIS -- A week ago, ahead of a deciding Game 3 against the Las Vegas Aces, Indiana Fever forward Myisha Hines-Allen laid out the franchise's expectations plainly.

"There's always going to be room for growth, but with how [GM] Amber [Cox] put this team together, it's championship or bust," Hines-Allen said before the game. "We're all trying to win this championship this year."

After a semifinal appearance in 2025, a season in which star Caitlin Clark sat out most of the year injured, hopes were high for 2026.

And sure enough, the Fever had the No. 1 offense in WNBA history, averaging 96.0 points per game in the regular season. Kelsey Mitchell (24.7 points per game) and Clark (22.3) finished ranked No. 2 and No. 3 in points per game and were the highest-scoring teammates in league history.

But throughout, off-court drama surrounded the team. Then a swoon in the final days of the regular season dropped the Fever to the No. 6 seed, facing the defending champion Aces in a best-of-three first round.

After the Game 3 loss, a back-and-forth affair, the Fever were left reckoning with a season that ended earlier than any of them hoped.

Within 48 hours of the season-ending loss, another controversy had developed: After Cox issued a strong defense of the Fever fanbase in her end-of-season availability, Mitchell seemed to contradict it, referencing troubling fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark. It was a fitting conclusion to a season of big dreams and bitter disappointments where the focus could never just be on basketball.

"Not every season's perfect," Aliyah Boston said Saturday after the season's end. "You're going to have your ups and downs, but we really stuck together through it all. Like no matter what. Obviously, when you look back at games that you wish that you didn't drop early, and maybe that would have been a difference. ... But here we are, right? There's nothing we can do right now."

ON THE COURT, at least one half of the Fever's plan went perfectly.
The offense was formidable, and Clark's return went better than anyone could have hoped. Mitchell set the league record for the most points scored (1,086) and the most 3-point field goals (135) while scoring 20-plus points in a WNBA-record 27 consecutive games. Boston was an All-Star for the fourth consecutive year with a career-high 16.1 points per game, grabbed 8.0 rebounds and extended her range beyond the 3-point line and shot 40.6%.

Clark was the first player in the history of the league to score 40-plus points with 10-plus assists in a single game; her five games of 30-plus points and 10-plus assists this season are more than any other player in league history combined. She became the league's first player to record 800-plus points and 300-plus assists in a single season.

Clark called 2026 one of the most fulfilling years of her career. She played more basketball than ever as she rehabbed. She played in Team USA camps, 40 regular-season games and was selected for the FIBA World Cup team that won gold in September. A worrisome back issue flared up early in the season but proved not to be a long-term issue. The defensive part of her game was highly criticized early in the season as teams specifically targeted her, but even that improved incrementally. A sneaky midrange game began to appear as the season went on to complement the drives to the basket and the step-back 3s.

Clark's first signature shoe with Nike, the Caitlin 1, released last week.

"I didn't play much last year, but I was able to come out here and put together the best season I've had," Clark said, "and perform at a really high level and basically get better in every area and still feel like I have so many areas to improve.

"I guess that's the most exciting part moving forward."

The old saying, though, goes that defense wins championships, and that was the problem all season for the Fever. They ranked No. 11 in points allowed per game (90.4) and No. 8 in defensive rating (108.3). The Aces scored 102 and 94 in Game 1 and 3 victories to eliminate Indiana.

And off the court, the Fever were constantly barraged with distractions or drama. For much of the season, it felt like those 40 minutes between the lines -- win or lose -- were the most peaceful, normal times of the summer for this group.

"Obviously, we weathered a lot," Clark said. "There's always so much outside noise and a microscope of how we perform every single day, and a lot of really good moments, a lot of tough moments, too."

SINCE CLARK WAS drafted No. 1 in 2024, the Fever have had an inordinate amount of attention on the organization from both WNBA fans and entities that rarely paid attention to the league in the past. Clark's name was recently, and randomly, brought up in the middle of a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing.

It's been a boon for the Fever, who have become the most popular team in the league thanks in large part to her fame -- quickly acknowledged by all those around the team, including Cox.

"The other piece about Caitlin that I never want to take for granted is just what she has meant to our team, what she has meant to the league, and what she's meant to women's basketball," she said. "She remains the tipping point. You look at the ratings and you look at the full buildings, that started in 2024 when she came into the league, and that is because of Caitlin Clark."

But it can also lead to increased scrutiny on Clark and the rest of the team, as happened multiple times this season.

In June, the relationship between Stephanie White and Clark was questioned after the coach was seen in an animated discussion with the point guard during a 16-point loss to the Portland Fire. Both downplayed it as two competitive people in the heat of the moment. Clark and assistant coach Briann January also had fiery interactions on the sideline that begat questions regarding the franchise player and the coaching staff.

The focus on the Fever's play -- and White -- continued throughout the season. Then, in June, Sophie Cunningham kicked off another round of headlines for the Fever. Cunningham, a popular personality on social media and her podcast, has no problem being an agitator. T-shirts featuring her pointing at DeWanna Bonner after a heated game against the Phoenix Mercury in June became a hot commodity at Fever games at home and on the road.

But one moment affected not only the Fever, but the entire league. In an ESPN article published in July, Cunningham discussed, among other things, how to "protect women's sports" and said: "I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

It became a seasonlong topic with coaches and players being asked their opinions around the league. Protests both for and against began forming outside arenas when the Fever would play on the road. Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton was suspended from attending five home games after her exchange with a pair of fans who brought signs into Climate Pledge Arena supporting Cunningham with the Fever in town for a road game in late July.

All these issues and more -- 11 Republican lawmakers sent WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert a letter in July demanding the league take "accountability" for "multiple attacks" against Clark -- came to a head just after the All-Star break.

In a game on Aug. 8, Cunningham took a hit around the head and neck on a fast-break layup from DiJonai Carrington. The particularly hard contact started a dustup on the court; Carrington was issued a flagrant 2 and ejected from the game. Moments later, Carrington posted on her Threads account: "WHITE PRIVILEGE @indianafever." Postgame, White acknowledged it was a hard foul, but said she didn't think Carrington intentionally went for the neck.

Fever fans accused White of not supporting her players. Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith tweeted, "Ok... The @IndianaFever need to let Stephanie White go. No solid coach would ever take the side of the opposing team's player who committed a flagrant foul on one of your own players. Terrible coaching! The Fever need to defend their players."

During the next home game, on Aug. 11 against the New York Liberty, boos rained down on Gainbridge Arena. The disdain was focused on White during pregame introductions. Before that game, White had used her pregame media session to respond to the noise; team president Kelly Krauskopf issued a statement with full support for White that same day.

"The hate, the fearmongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win," White said before the game, pounding her fist on a table multiple times.

"We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," she added. "Every day, these women put their ass on the line. Every day, when they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win, humility will win, and kindness will win. I stand by them. I will always stand by them.

"Everybody else can go to hell."

EVERY SEASON WITH Clark on the team will have championship expectations, a side effect of having a generational player on the roster. But every season with Clark, through no fault of her own, also brings a level of outside noise that organizations will have to navigate.

That was evident on Saturday, during Mitchell's end-of-season availability.

Compared with her interviews after the Game 3 loss, the weight seemed lifted from Mitchell's shoulders as she smiled and acknowledged that she would be "selfish" in her approach to unrestricted free agency.

Mitchell -- the Fever's No. 2 player in points and assists, No. 1 in 3-point field goals and No. 4 in steals in franchise history -- said it's hard to play in Indiana due to fan behavior and the intense microscope that comes with playing alongside Clark.

"Showing up every day to compete for fans that may or may not like you is hard," Mitchell said.

Earlier Saturday, in her own availability, Cox had effusively praised Clark and ended her session with a staunch defense of Fever fans that have received criticism for their behavior toward opposing players.

"The attacks on our fanbase have no basis in reality, and they need to stop," she said.

(Former Fever player Brianna Turner, now a member of the Aces, disputed Cox's sentiments on social media. "This is an unequivocally false statement," wrote Turner, who serves as treasurer of the Women's National Basketball Players Association. "Players inside and outside the organization have repeatedly issued complaints with the Fever fanbase. While it's not all Indy fans, it's certainly a trend. To say the attacks have 'no basis in reality' is disingenuous.")

Along with Mitchell, Cunningham, Tyasha Harris and Hines-Allen are all unrestricted free agents this winter -- meaning, like everything in the orbit of the Fever, the offseason could be dramatic.

Cox has said her priority is bringing back Mitchell and keeping the Fever's Big Three together.

Clark's play has made her eligible for the "EPIC" (Exceptional Performance on Initial Contract) provision of the new collective bargaining agreement that allows players to renegotiate the fourth year of their rookie deal and sign a three-year extension. Players that have been named all-WNBA first team or second team are eligible for a max deal or the supermax if named MVP.

"Caitlin has earned the opportunity to sign her EPIC extension, so we're really excited to talk to her and her team about that," Cox said. "She had an MVP-caliber season, and it was wonderful to see coming off of her injury."

As for Cunningham, Cox said the off-court conversations surrounding her will not impact the evaluation of the player. Through the first two months of the season, Cunningham was considered a Sixth Player of the Year candidate before she cooled over the last two months. Both Cox and White pointed to help on the wing as an offseason priority.

"Sophie's had two really productive years for us in terms of shooting the basketball," Cox said. "She is a really solid leader in the locker room, a great connector. She brings levity, but also brings a lot of experience. She's serious and is an important voice in our locker room when we need it. When we really need to lock in.

"She's an unrestricted free agent, so we look forward to having those conversations. Again, she had a really productive year, and we'll see just where things take us."

White, too, will be part of the conversations about the Fever's future. She just finished her second year at the helm, and 2025 was considered an overachievement, advancing to within one game of the Finals with an infirmary ward of a roster. The last five months have been considered a disappointment with a first-round exit and questions swirling around her job stability.

"There were some highlights, and there are things we never need to get better at," Cox said after the season. "We're all going to get in the room and get back to the drawing board and we're going to address some of those and make sure that we're ready to go when next season starts. And that includes Steph and the coaching staff."

"I feel support from the organization, no doubt about that," White said after the season. "At the end of the day, it's their decision about whether I return or not. I'd love the opportunity. I love this this franchise. I have always felt supported from this franchise, and I hope to continue to be the coach."

This all awaits Cox in what will undoubtedly be another busy offseason. A new practice facility is scheduled to open before 2027 training camp. Cox wants to add frontcourt depth to help Boston and Makayla Timpson, and a three-and-D wing is also on the wish list. Despite expectations, the Fever were light on playoff experience and there's optimism that it was gained the hard way. The hope is to continue to develop the young talent, build through the draft and supplement through free agency.

After a season with unfulfilled goals and more drama than anyone was thrilled about, there's an understandable wonder of how much could change.

"When you talk about the noise around this team, I think that's just a product of becoming mainstream," Cox said. "People care. I've been a part of this league for many, many years, and you could have a trade, you could have a bad loss and nobody cared. Nobody was writing about it. Nobody was tweeting about it, and that was bad. Apathy was bad.

"So, what comes with the quote-unquote noise? I would call it just a lot of people caring."
